people.story:
Giuseppe Circelli is known from one line. When his daughter Maria Donata married in January 1884, the clerk recorded her as the daughter "del fu Giuseppe", the late Giuseppe, who had lived in the town during his lifetime.[^marriage-1884] By then he was dead, and so was his wife.

Because neither parent was alive, the act records that consent to the marriage came from the bride's family council, the consiglio di famiglia, a group of relatives who stood in for parents who had died.[^marriage-1884]

That is all the records in this collection say about him. His age, his trade and his date of death are not known. Circelli was a common surname in San Bartolomeo in Galdo, and the town's civil registers survive on the Antenati portal, so his death record, and perhaps his marriage, should be findable there.[^research-md]

Update, November 2026. Giuseppe's own story now begins in the town's oldest civil registers. He was twenty-three, a farmer, when he promised himself in marriage to Anna Rita Mansolino on 17 January 1850; the clerk noted that his parents, Donato Circelli and Vincenza, had both died.[^marriage-circelli-mansolino-1850] On 3 January 1860 he registered twin daughters, Maria Filomena and Maria Lucia, and on 25 September 1863, at ten in the morning, he brought his new daughter Maria Donata to be recorded. She was baptized that same day.[^birth-circelli-twins-1860][^birth-maria-donata-1863]

Update, November 2026: his own birth act has now been found. On 13 February 1827 his father, Donato Circelli, a farm worker of forty-two from Strada Borgo Nuovo, came to the town hall to say that his wife Vincenza, also forty-two, had given birth to a boy the day before, 12 February, in the rented house where they lived. The boy was named Giuseppe, and the parish priest sent word the next day that he had been baptized.[^birth-giuseppe-circelli-1827] Giuseppe and his wife Anna Rita were born two years and about a week apart, in the same small town.

Giuseppe lost both parents young. His father Donato died on 8 November 1839, when Giuseppe was twelve, and his mother Vincenza on 18 October 1843, when he was sixteen.[^death-donato-circelli-1839][^death-vincenza-minichillo-1843]

media.transcription:
ATTI DI MATRIMONIO. Numero 16. [Margin:] Belfiore Lionardantonio / Circelli Maria Donata

L'anno milleottocento ottantaquattro addì ventisette di gennaio a ore anti meridiane nove e minuti cinquantacinque, nella Casa comunale di Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, aperta al pubblico.

Avanti di me Mosa [o Morra?] Giuseppe, Sindaco, Uffiziale dello Stato Civile, vestito in forma ufficiale sono personalmente comparsi:

1. Belfiore Lionardantonio, di anni ventitre, contadino, nato in Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, residente in detto Comune, figlio di padre ignoto, residente in [vuoto], e di madre ignota, residente in [vuoto];

2. Circelli Maria Donata, di anni ventuno, contadina, nata in Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, residente in detto Comune, figlia del fu Giuseppe, residente in vita qui, e della fu Mansolina [lettura incerta] Mita, residente in vita in detto Comune,

i quali mi hanno richiesto di unirli in matrimonio: a questo effetto mi hanno presentato il documento sotto descritto; e dall'esame di questo, nonchè di quelli già prodotti all'atto della richiesta delle pubblicazioni, i quali tutti, muniti del mio visto, inserisco nel volume degli allegati a questo registro, risultandomi nulla ostare alla celebrazione del loro matrimonio, ho letto agli sposi gli articoli centotrenta, centotrentuno e centotrentadue del Codice Civile, e quindi ho domandato allo sposo se intende di prendere in moglie la qui presente Circelli Maria Donata, e a questa se intende di prendere in marito il qui presente Belfiore Lionardantonio, ed avendomi ciascuno risposto affermativamente a piena intelligenza anche dei testimoni sotto indicati, ho pronunziato in nome della legge che i medesimi sono uniti in matrimonio.

A quest'atto sono stati presenti Reino [lettura incerta] Domenico, di anni quarantasei, guardia municipale, e Paradiso Giuseppe, di anni sessantasette, donzello municipale, entrambi residenti in questo Comune.

Il documento presentato è il certificato delle pubblicazioni da me eseguite, la prima il tredici e la seconda il venti del corrente mese di gennaio. Al matrimonio suddetto è stato prestato il consenso dal consiglio di famiglia della sposa, come risulta dall'atto di richiesta delle pubblicazioni.

Letto il presente atto agl'intervenuti, si sono meco sottoscritti i soli testimoni, essendo gli altri analfabeti.

[Firme:] Reino Domenico, testimone. Giuseppe Paradiso, testimonio. Giuseppe Mora [?]
media.translation:
MARRIAGE RECORDS. Number 16. [Margin:] Belfiore Lionardantonio / Circelli Maria Donata

In the year eighteen hundred eighty-four, on the twenty-seventh of January, at nine fifty-five in the morning, in the town hall of San Bartolomeo in Galdo, open to the public.

Before me, Giuseppe Mosa [or Morra?], Mayor and Civil Registrar, dressed in official form, there personally appeared:

1. Lionardantonio Belfiore, aged twenty-three, farm worker (contadino), born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo and living in that town, son of an unknown father and an unknown mother (padre ignoto, madre ignota);

2. Maria Donata Circelli, aged twenty-one, farm worker (contadina), born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo and living in that town, daughter of the late Giuseppe, who lived here in his lifetime, and of the late Mansolina [uncertain reading] Mita, who lived in this town in her lifetime,

who asked me to unite them in marriage. For this purpose they presented the document described below. Having examined it, and those already produced when the banns were requested, all of which I have stamped and placed in the volume of attachments to this register, and finding no impediment to the marriage, I read to the couple articles 130, 131 and 132 of the Civil Code. I then asked the groom whether he wished to take as his wife Maria Donata Circelli, here present, and asked her whether she wished to take as her husband Lionardantonio Belfiore, here present. Each answered yes, in the full hearing of the witnesses named below, and I pronounced them united in marriage in the name of the law.

Present at this act were Domenico Reino [uncertain reading], aged forty-six, municipal guard, and Giuseppe Paradiso, aged sixty-seven, municipal usher, both living in this town.

The document presented is the certificate of the banns I published, the first on the thirteenth and the second on the twentieth of this month of January. Consent to the marriage was given by the bride's family council, as shown in the act requesting the banns.

This act was read to those present. Only the witnesses signed it with me, the others being illiterate.

[Signatures:] Domenico Reino, witness. Giuseppe Paradiso, witness. Giuseppe Mora [?]

people.summary: Maria Donata's mother. Records from 1850, 1860 and 1863 name her Anna Rita (or Rita) Mansolino; earlier research on this site read her name as Marianna Mita.
people.story:
Maria Donata's marriage act of January 1884 names her mother with the word fu, "the late", and records that she too had lived in San Bartolomeo in Galdo.[^marriage-1884]

Her name needs care. Earlier research on this site gave it as Marianna Mita.[^research-md] A close reading of the scan for this profile does not clearly support Marianna: the handwriting looks more like Mansolina or Marsolina, followed by a short surname that reads as Mita. Old Italian civil hands are hard to read, and a second record would settle it. Until then the tree keeps "Marianna Mita" and marks the name as uncertain.[^marriage-1884]

Nothing else is known about her yet: not her age, her parents, or when she died.

Update, November 2026. Three more records have now been found, and they help with her name. When she married Giuseppe Circelli on 17 January 1850 she was Anna Rita Mansolino, twenty-one, the daughter of Francesco Mansolino, a farmer, and of Brigida.[^marriage-circelli-mansolino-1850] Ten years later she was "Rita Manzolino" when her twin girls were born, and "Rita Mansolino" again at Maria Donata's birth in 1863.[^birth-circelli-twins-1860][^birth-maria-donata-1863] That fits the fresh reading of the 1884 act above, which saw "Mansolina" in the handwriting. The tree now shows her as Anna Rita Mansolino and keeps Marianna Mita as the name earlier research gave her.

Update, November 2026: in January 1851 her husband registered their daughter Antonia and named the mother as Margarita Mansolino, twenty-three.[^birth-antonia-circelli-1851] Rita is the usual short form of Margherita, the husband and the age agree, so Margarita, Anna Rita and Rita are the same woman. Antonia is the eldest child of the marriage found so far.

Update, November 2026: her own birth act has now been found. On 20 February 1829 her father, Francesco Mansolino, a farm worker of thirty-five, came to the town hall and declared that his wife Brigida, thirty-eight, had given birth to a daughter that morning. The baby was named Anna Rita, and the parish priest sent word the next day that she had been baptized under that name.[^birth-anna-rita-mansolino-1829] So Anna Rita was her baptismal name, and Rita and Margarita were what the clerks later wrote.

people.summary: A foundling who married Maria Donata Circelli in San Bartolomeo in Galdo in 1884. The working identification is that he is Anthony Belfiore, father of nine children in New Rochelle, who died there in 1938.
people.story:
At five minutes to ten on the morning of January 27, 1884, a twenty-three-year-old farm worker stood in the town hall of San Bartolomeo in Galdo to be married. The clerk wrote his name as Belfiore Lionardantonio. In the spaces for his parents he wrote two phrases: padre ignoto, madre ignota. Father unknown, mother unknown.[^marriage-1884]

Those phrases explain the family name. A child of unknown parents had no surname to inherit, so one was given to him. In Italy such children were often left at the ruota degli esposti, the turning wheel set into the wall of a church or hospital, and the institution or the registrar chose their names.[^ctx-ruota] Some foundling surnames marked the child as abandoned, such as Esposito. Others were simply pleasant words, and Belfiore, "beautiful flower", reads like one of these. That is very probably how Leonardantonio came by it, although his own birth and admission records have not been found. It also means the family has no link to the noble Belfiore families of other parts of Italy. The name begins with him.[^research-md]

## The wedding

The marriage act says he was born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo and lived there. His bride was Maria Donata Circelli, twenty-one, also a farm worker, whose parents were both dead. Her consent came from a council of her relatives. The banns had been read on the 13th and the 20th of January. Two town employees stood as witnesses: a municipal guard aged forty-six and the town hall usher, aged sixty-seven. When the act was read back, only the witnesses signed, "the others being illiterate".[^marriage-1884]

## From Leonardantonio to Anthony

No record in this collection uses the name Leonardantonio after 1884. In America the children's father is Anthony or Antonio. The working identification on this site is that he is the same man. It is a strong case but not a proven one, and it rests on several records that point the same way.

- **The name.** Leonardantonio joins Leonardo and Antonio. Using only Antonio, and then Anthony, is an ordinary change for an Italian immigrant.
- **The children's records.** Michael's 1952 death certificate names his parents as Anthony Belfiore and Maria Circelli.[^death-michael-1952] Sammy's obituary calls the nine children's parents "the late Anthony and Maria Cicelli Belfiore".[^standard-star-obit] Indexed records give Frank's and Lena's parents as Antonio Belfiore and Maria D. Circelli.[^frank-index][^lena-index]
- **Citizenship.** In 1918 Michael answered the citizenship question in the column for men who became citizens through their father's naturalization while still minors, writing "Father Papers".[^ww1-michael] His father, then, was in the United States and naturalized before Michael turned twenty-one, around 1906.
- **A return voyage.** Earlier research found a 1909 Ellis Island manifest listing a "Belfiore, Antonio" from San Bartolomeo as a US citizen returning from Italy.[^manifest-1909]
- **A death.** The New York State death index lists an Anthony Belfiore who died in New Rochelle on July 11, 1938, certificate 42184.[^ny-death-index-1938]

Earlier versions of this site argued that Leonardantonio died in Italy before 1896, because Maria Donata crossed that year under her own surname. The records point the other way. Italian women kept their birth surnames in civil and travel records, so a list naming her as Circelli says nothing about her husband. And Frank, born in New Rochelle in November 1897, and Sammy, born there on Christmas Day 1899, both had a father named Anthony or Antonio.[^frank-index][^standard-star-obit]

## What we do not know

When he left San Bartolomeo, and on which ship, is unknown. The transcription of Michael's death certificate gives Michael 58 years of residence in New Rochelle, which would put Michael's arrival around 1894, two years before Maria Donata's crossing.[^death-michael-1952] Whether father and son came first is a fair question, and the 1900 census should answer it, because it asked every immigrant the year they arrived.

His burial place is also unknown. Holy Sepulchre Cemetery in New Rochelle, where Michael was buried, is the first place to ask.

Update, November 2026. He did come to America, and early. Two days before Christmas 1890 a "Leonardo Belfiori" of twenty-nine, from San Bartolomeo, landed in New York on the Hindoustan.[^hindoustan-1890-manifest] In June 1900 the census found him in New Rochelle as Antonio, born in September 1861, married sixteen years, here since 1890 and already a citizen.[^census-1900] Every detail fits the young man who married Maria Donata in 1884.[^marriage-1884] Over the next thirty years the census takers wrote him down as Tony, Anthony and Antonio: a day laborer in 1900, the keeper of a saloon in 1915, a mason in 1925, and by 1920 the owner of the family home.[^census-1905][^census-1915][^census-1920][^census-1925][^census-1930]

Update, November 2026: where the family lived. The census takers wrote down the family's front doors as well as their names. In June 1900 they rented a house at 13 Lawton Street. In 1905 they were at house 62 on a street that looks like Cottage Place. By 1910 Antonio owned 41 Brook Street, with a mortgage, and kept his saloon; the family was still at 41 Brook in 1915 and when Sammy registered for the draft in 1918. In January 1920 the census gives 54 Brook Street, again owned (the numbers on the street may have changed in between). In 1925 they were at 39 Albemarle, and by 1930 Antonio and Marie owned 55 Potter Avenue, a house the census valued at $35,000, with a radio in the parlour.[^census-1900][^census-1905][^census-1910][^census-1915][^ww1-samuel][^census-1920][^census-1925][^census-1930] Brook Street stayed in the family's life: in 1930 their son Michael was renting at 52 Brook Street, a few doors from the old home.[^census-1930-michael]

Update, November 2026: three new pieces. First, his age. He was twenty-three at his wedding in January 1884 and still twenty-three when he registered Michael's birth that December, and twenty-nine when he landed in New York in December 1890. Put together, those ages point to a birth around January 1861.[^marriage-1884][^birth-michele-1884][^hindoustan-1890-manifest] The town's register of births for 1861 is the one year not yet online, which would explain why he has never turned up in the 1860 index.

Second, his name. In March 1882 the midwife of San Bartolomeo reported a baby girl, born dead, "to a woman who does not consent to be named", and the officer wrote that the child was given the name Rosa "and the surname Belfiore".[^birth-rosa-belfiore-1882] It suggests that in this town Belfiore was a surname the civil office gave to children whose parents were not named. Leonardantonio, recorded as son of an unknown father and an unknown mother, very likely received his surname the same way. That is a reasonable reading of the evidence, not yet a proof.

Third, his American paperwork. The Westchester County Archives index lists an Antonio "Belfiora" (once written Zelfiora) who filed a declaration of intention in 1896 and a naturalization petition in 1899, which fits the citizen of the 1900 census and Michael's draft card, where Michael said he was a citizen through his father's papers.[^westchester-naturalization-index][^census-1900][^ww1-michael] The same archives hold a will filed in 1938 for Antonio Belfiore of New Rochelle, the year Anthony Belfiore died there.[^westchester-surrogates-index] Neither document has been seen yet; both are worth a copy request, because a will would name his children.

media.transcription:
ATTI DI MATRIMONIO. Numero 16. [Margin:] Belfiore Lionardantonio / Circelli Maria Donata

L'anno milleottocento ottantaquattro addì ventisette di gennaio a ore anti meridiane nove e minuti cinquantacinque, nella Casa comunale di Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, aperta al pubblico.

Avanti di me Mosa [o Morra?] Giuseppe, Sindaco, Uffiziale dello Stato Civile, vestito in forma ufficiale sono personalmente comparsi:

1. Belfiore Lionardantonio, di anni ventitre, contadino, nato in Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, residente in detto Comune, figlio di padre ignoto, residente in [vuoto], e di madre ignota, residente in [vuoto];

2. Circelli Maria Donata, di anni ventuno, contadina, nata in Sanbartolomeo in Galdo, residente in detto Comune, figlia del fu Giuseppe, residente in vita qui, e della fu Mansolina [lettura incerta] Mita, residente in vita in detto Comune,

i quali mi hanno richiesto di unirli in matrimonio: a questo effetto mi hanno presentato il documento sotto descritto; e dall'esame di questo, nonchè di quelli già prodotti all'atto della richiesta delle pubblicazioni, i quali tutti, muniti del mio visto, inserisco nel volume degli allegati a questo registro, risultandomi nulla ostare alla celebrazione del loro matrimonio, ho letto agli sposi gli articoli centotrenta, centotrentuno e centotrentadue del Codice Civile, e quindi ho domandato allo sposo se intende di prendere in moglie la qui presente Circelli Maria Donata, e a questa se intende di prendere in marito il qui presente Belfiore Lionardantonio, ed avendomi ciascuno risposto affermativamente a piena intelligenza anche dei testimoni sotto indicati, ho pronunziato in nome della legge che i medesimi sono uniti in matrimonio.

A quest'atto sono stati presenti Reino [lettura incerta] Domenico, di anni quarantasei, guardia municipale, e Paradiso Giuseppe, di anni sessantasette, donzello municipale, entrambi residenti in questo Comune.

Il documento presentato è il certificato delle pubblicazioni da me eseguite, la prima il tredici e la seconda il venti del corrente mese di gennaio. Al matrimonio suddetto è stato prestato il consenso dal consiglio di famiglia della sposa, come risulta dall'atto di richiesta delle pubblicazioni.

Letto il presente atto agl'intervenuti, si sono meco sottoscritti i soli testimoni, essendo gli altri analfabeti.

[Firme:] Reino Domenico, testimone. Giuseppe Paradiso, testimonio. Giuseppe Mora [?]
media.translation:
MARRIAGE RECORDS. Number 16. [Margin:] Belfiore Lionardantonio / Circelli Maria Donata

In the year eighteen hundred eighty-four, on the twenty-seventh of January, at nine fifty-five in the morning, in the town hall of San Bartolomeo in Galdo, open to the public.

Before me, Giuseppe Mosa [or Morra?], Mayor and Civil Registrar, dressed in official form, there personally appeared:

1. Lionardantonio Belfiore, aged twenty-three, farm worker (contadino), born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo and living in that town, son of an unknown father and an unknown mother (padre ignoto, madre ignota);

2. Maria Donata Circelli, aged twenty-one, farm worker (contadina), born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo and living in that town, daughter of the late Giuseppe, who lived here in his lifetime, and of the late Mansolina [uncertain reading] Mita, who lived in this town in her lifetime,

who asked me to unite them in marriage. For this purpose they presented the document described below. Having examined it, and those already produced when the banns were requested, all of which I have stamped and placed in the volume of attachments to this register, and finding no impediment to the marriage, I read to the couple articles 130, 131 and 132 of the Civil Code. I then asked the groom whether he wished to take as his wife Maria Donata Circelli, here present, and asked her whether she wished to take as her husband Lionardantonio Belfiore, here present. Each answered yes, in the full hearing of the witnesses named below, and I pronounced them united in marriage in the name of the law.

Present at this act were Domenico Reino [uncertain reading], aged forty-six, municipal guard, and Giuseppe Paradiso, aged sixty-seven, municipal usher, both living in this town.

The document presented is the certificate of the banns I published, the first on the thirteenth and the second on the twentieth of this month of January. Consent to the marriage was given by the bride's family council, as shown in the act requesting the banns.

This act was read to those present. Only the witnesses signed it with me, the others being illiterate.

[Signatures:] Domenico Reino, witness. Giuseppe Paradiso, witness. Giuseppe Mora [?]

people.summary: Born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo around 1862, married Leonardantonio Belfiore in 1884, and crossed to New York on the SS Oregon in December 1896. She raised nine children in New Rochelle.
people.story:
Maria Donata Circelli could not write her name. When she married in January 1884 she was twenty-one, a farm worker, and an orphan: the clerk wrote both her parents' names after the word fu, "the late". With her parents dead, the consent for her marriage came from a council of her relatives.[^marriage-1884]

She was born in San Bartolomeo in Galdo, a hill town in the province of Benevento, where Circelli is one of the old family names.[^marriage-1884][^research-md] Her husband was Leonardantonio Belfiore, a foundling two years older. Their son Michele, later Michael, was born on 15 December 1884, eleven months after the wedding.[^birth-michele-1884]

## The crossing

On December 2, 1896, the steamship Oregon reached New York from Genoa and Naples. On its passenger list, at line 413, was "Circelli, Maria Doreta". Earlier research recorded her age as 34, which agrees with the marriage act.[^oregon-1896-index] Doreta is very probably a clerk's version of Donata, and the source of the "Maria D." in later records.

She traveled under her own surname. That was normal for an Italian married woman, whose legal surname did not change at marriage, and it should not be read as a sign that she was a widow. Her arrival came in the last months of the first Ellis Island station, a wooden complex that burned in June 1897. Most passenger manifests from those years were lost in the fire. Lists like hers survive because the Customs Service kept its own copies.[^ctx-ellis-nps][^ctx-ellis-foundation]

Whether Michael crossed with her is not known. The full list page would show any child on the lines after hers. The page shared on this site as the Oregon list does not include her line.[^customs-list-page]

## New Rochelle

By November 1897 the family was in New Rochelle, New York, where Frank was born. Sammy followed on Christmas Day 1899.[^frank-index][^standard-star-obit] In all she raised nine children who survived to be named in Sammy's obituary: Michael, Frank, Joseph and Sammy, and Rose, Caroline, Mollie, Phyl and Mary.[^standard-star-obit] Three of the sons became golf professionals.[^standard-star-obit]

Her Circelli relatives used the same route. In March 1898 Salvatore and Michele Circelli arrived on the Alsatia, giving San Bartolomeo as their home, and in 1911 Salvatore gave New Rochelle as his destination.[^alsatia-1898][^santanna-1911] How they were related to her is not yet known.

## What we do not know

Her date and place of death have not been found. By 1972 Sammy's obituary could call his parents "the late Anthony and Maria".[^standard-star-obit] A New York death certificate under Maria, Mary or Marie Belfiore, or a burial record at Holy Sepulchre Cemetery in New Rochelle, would give the date, and should name her parents, which would help settle her mother's name.

Update, November 2026. Maria Donata's own birth record has been found. On 25 September 1863, at ten in the morning, Giuseppe Circelli, a farmer of thirty-six, carried his new daughter to the town hall of San Bartolomeo in Galdo; her mother was Rita Mansolino. They named her Maria Donata, and she was baptized that same day.[^birth-maria-donata-1863] She had two older sisters, twins born in 1860.[^birth-circelli-twins-1860]

She did not cross the ocean alone. The full page of the Oregon's list shows three children with her: Michele, twelve, and two little girls written as Francesca, nine, and Anna, six.[^oregon-1896-manifest] The New Rochelle censuses show who they were: Filomena, the family's Phyl, and Mary.[^census-1900][^census-1905] By 1900 she was the mother of six living children, and the house went on filling for another eight years.[^census-1900][^census-1915] The state death index records a Marie D. Belfiore who died in New Rochelle on 26 September 1937, the day after her seventy-fourth birthday.[^nysdi-1937]

In 1910 she told the census taker she had borne nine children and that all nine were living, the same nine that the family has always counted.[^census-1910]

Update, November 2026: her homes in New Rochelle. Maria Donata kept house at 13 Lawton Street in 1900, at house 62 in 1905, at 41 Brook Street in 1910 and 1915, at 54 Brook Street in 1920, at 39 Albemarle in 1925 and at 55 Potter Avenue, the family's own house, in 1930.[^census-1900][^census-1905][^census-1910][^census-1915][^census-1920][^census-1925][^census-1930]

people.story:
Salvatore Circelli crossed from Naples on the Alsatia, which sailed on February 26, 1898, and reached New York on March 19. He was twenty-eight and could not read or write. On the next line was Michele Circelli, twenty-five. Several men from San Bartolomeo were listed together on that page, and the clerk wrote the town as "S. Bartolomeo in Calore".[^alsatia-1898][^alsatia-1898-index]

Thirteen years later he crossed again. The Sant'Anna left Naples on November 14, 1911, carrying a married Salvatore Circelli, forty-two, whose final destination was New Rochelle, New York.[^santanna-1911] His two ages agree on a birth around 1869, and the second voyage ties a Circelli of San Bartolomeo directly to the town where Maria Donata's family lived.

## How was he related to Maria Donata?

Earlier research called him her brother or cousin. An online index of San Bartolomeo births lists a Salvatore born on January 1, 1869, and a Michele born on March 12, 1871, both sons of Leonardo Circelli and Rosa Pacifico.[^italyheritage-circelli] If those are the two men on the Alsatia, they were not Maria Donata's brothers, because her parents were Giuseppe Circelli and his wife. They could be cousins. The ages do not match perfectly for Michele, and the index has not been checked against the registers, so the relationship stays open.

Update, November 2026: his marriage act has now been read on the original page. On 27 March 1893 Salvatore Circelli, twenty-four, a farm worker born in San Bartolomeo, son of Leonardo and Rosa Pacifico, married Maria Carmela Petrilli, sixteen, daughter of Michele Petrilli. Salvatore signed his own name.[^marriage-circelli-petrilli-1893] That confirms what the online index said about his parents, so he was not Maria Donata's brother. Children named Donato (1894) and Maria Bambina (1897) followed in the town's registers. His wife's name fits the "Maria Circelli" given as his wife on the 1911 crossing, so he is very likely the same Salvatore. Whether Leonardo Circelli was a brother or cousin of Maria Donata's father Giuseppe is still open.

people.story:
Michele Circelli was twenty-five when he reached New York on the Alsatia on March 19, 1898, on the line after Salvatore Circelli. Like Salvatore he could not read or write, and his home was given as San Bartolomeo.[^alsatia-1898][^alsatia-1898-index]

He is sometimes confused with Michael Belfiore, because Michele is the Italian form of Michael. He cannot be the same man. Michael was born in December 1884 and would have been thirteen in 1898, and he was a Belfiore, not a Circelli.[^birth-michele-1884]

An online index of San Bartolomeo births lists a Michele Circelli born on March 12, 1871, son of Leonardo Circelli and Rosa Pacifico.[^italyheritage-circelli] That child would have been twenty-six or twenty-seven in March 1898, close to but not exactly the age on the manifest. If he is the same man, he was probably Maria Donata's cousin rather than her brother. Nothing more is known of him yet.

people.summary: The eldest son and the only one of the four brothers born in Italy. A house painter in New Rochelle for most of his life, married twice, and Seb's great-grandfather.
people.story:
Michael Kirtus Belfiore registered for the draft on September 12, 1918, the day the United States called up every man from 18 to 45.[^ctx-ww1-draft] The registrar described him as of medium height and medium build, with brown eyes and black hair. He was thirty-two, a painter, living at 114 Winyah Avenue in New Rochelle and working for an employer whose name reads as Witmark, at 8 Banks Street.[^ww1-michael]

Two answers on that card matter more than the rest. For citizenship he wrote "Father Papers", in the column for men who became citizens through a father's naturalization before they turned twenty-one. And as his nearest relative he named "(Child) Dorothy Belfiore" of 216 Hamilton Street, Bridgeport, Connecticut.[^ww1-michael] He signed the card himself: Michael, then a word he struck out, then Belfiore, with Kirtus written underneath.

## Born in Italy

He was born on 15 December 1884 at a quarter past ten in the morning, in the family house at no. 17 of a lane whose name reads as Vico Passaro, in San Bartolomeo in Galdo. Two days later his father Leonardantonio, twenty-three, carried him to the town hall to be registered.[^birth-michele-1884] His American papers never quite agreed: the 1918 card and the transcription of his death certificate say 1885, and his 1942 card says 1883.[^ww1-michael][^death-michael-1952][^ww2-michael] The Italian act, written down two days after he was born, settles it.

He was the only one of the four brothers born in Italy.[^standard-star-obit] When he crossed is unknown. His death certificate gives 58 years of residence, which would mean about 1894.[^death-michael-1952] The 1940 census recorded him as naturalized, which matches the 1918 card: he became a citizen through his father.[^census-1940][^ww1-michael]

## Two marriages

Dorothy, the child named on the 1918 card, was living in Bridgeport, apart from her father. Family knowledge holds that she was the daughter of an earlier marriage. The first wife's name is not known.[^family-knowledge]

His second wife was Frances Towey, an Irish-American born in New York in 1897.[^ssdi-frances][^family-knowledge] In April 1940 the census found them at 488 North Avenue, New Rochelle, with their sons Edward, nineteen, and Joseph, seventeen. Michael had left school after seventh grade. He was out of work and had been looking for thirty-six weeks; in 1939 he had worked sixteen weeks as a building painter and earned $200. Frances worked twenty hours a week in a high school cafeteria and had earned $420. Joseph, still in school, worked as a grocery delivery boy.[^census-1940]

## The non-golfing brother

While his three younger brothers became golf professionals at clubs from Daytona Beach to Grosse Pointe, Michael stayed in New Rochelle and painted. Sammy's obituary called him "their non-golfing brother".[^standard-star-obit]

In April 1942 he registered again, in the "old man's registration" for men born between 1877 and 1897.[^ctx-ww2-fourth] He lived at 48 Coligni Avenue and had no telephone. His employer was Alfred A. Last of 141 Chauncey Avenue. The person who would always know his address was "Wife, same address".[^ww2-michael]

He died at New Rochelle Hospital on January 16, 1952, of arteriosclerotic heart disease, and was buried at Holy Sepulchre Cemetery three days later. Frances was the informant on his death certificate. His last address was 46 Mechanic Street.[^death-michael-1952] His grandson William, Seb's uncle, was not yet two.[^family-william]

Update, November 2026. Michael crossed with his mother on the Oregon in December 1896, a boy of twelve listed as Michele.[^oregon-1896-manifest] In Italy, the 1884 birth index for San Bartolomeo lists "Belfiore Michele Antonio, son of Leonardantonio" as act 440, a number beyond the 417 acts of the main register, so the act sits in a supplementary register that is not online.[^index-births-1884] His cards and censuses give 1883 and 1885, so the act itself, once it could be read, would settle his year.

Two more censuses tell us about the years between his marriages. In January 1920 Michael was a widower of thirty-four, lodging with a family in New Rochelle and managing a bowling alley of his own; the same census also lists a "Mike", thirty-six, at his parents' home, very likely the same man counted twice.[^census-1920-michael][^census-1920] By 1930 he was married to Frances, working again as a house painter, with Dorothy, seventeen, and the boys Edward and Joseph at home.[^census-1930-michael] On that census he gave his age at first marriage as thirty-seven, which seems to describe his marriage to Frances about 1920 rather than his first.

Update, November 2026: Michael's addresses. In 1900 and 1905 he lived with his parents on Lawton Street and at house 62. In 1920, a widower, he lodged on North Avenue with John and Margaret Stephens; twenty years later his own family lived at 488 North Avenue. In 1930 he, Frances and the children rented 52 Brook Street, a few doors from 41 and 54 Brook, where his parents had lived.[^census-1900][^census-1905][^census-1920-michael][^census-1930-michael][^census-1940] In 1950 the census found him, aged sixty-five, at home with Frances and Edward.[^census-1950-frances]

Update, November 2026: Michael's birth act has been found and read. It is act 440 of the 1884 births, and it turned out to be online after all, on the 18th page of the register as Antenati now shows it. On 17 December 1884 his father Leonardantonio, twenty-three and a farm worker, came to the town hall to report that his wife Donata Circelli had given birth to a boy at a quarter past ten in the morning of 15 December, at home, at number 17 of a lane whose name reads like Vico Passaro.[^birth-michele-1884] So Michael was born on 15 December 1884, the date his draft cards remembered, in the year that sits between the two years they gave. One of the two witnesses was Antonia Circelli, daughter of the late Giuseppe: his mother's elder sister, his aunt. Nobody in the room but the officer could write.

people.summary: An Irish-American born in New York in 1897, Michael's second wife and the mother of Edward and Joseph. She died in New Rochelle in 1967.
people.story:
Frances Towey was born on September 17, 1897, in New York.[^ssdi-frances][^census-1940] Towey is an Irish surname, and the family remembers her as Irish-American.[^family-knowledge] Her parents' names have not been found yet. Her death certificate, which has been ordered, should give them and their birthplaces.

She married Michael Belfiore, who was about twelve years older and had a daughter from an earlier marriage. The date is not known, but their son Edward was born around 1920.[^census-1940]

In April 1940 she was forty-two, had finished eighth grade, and was working twenty hours a week in a high school cafeteria. She had earned $420 the year before, more than Michael, who was out of work. The family lived at 488 North Avenue, New Rochelle, with their sons Edward and Joseph.[^census-1940]

When Michael died in January 1952, she gave the details for his death certificate as Frances M. Belfiore, of 46 Mechanic Street.[^death-michael-1952] She died in New Rochelle on April 5, 1967, aged sixty-nine.[^ssdi-frances]

Update, November 2026. Her parents have been found. Frances, called Fannie as a girl, was the eldest child of James Towey, an Irish immigrant who came in 1887 and worked in a machine shop, and his Irish-born wife Margaret. The 1900 census gives her birth as September 1897 in New York, and she grew up in New Rochelle with her brothers James and John and her sister Mary.[^census-1900-towey][^census-1910-towey] She married Michael about 1920, when she was about twenty-two, and became stepmother to his daughter Dorothy.[^census-1930-michael]

Update, November 2026: the Towey homes, and a brother next door. In 1900 the Toweys lived at 200 Horton Avenue and in 1910 at 47 Oak Street, both in New Rochelle; in 1930 Frances and Michael rented 52 Brook Street.[^census-1900-towey][^census-1910-towey][^census-1930-michael] In April 1950 her son Joseph and his wife Dorothy had a John J. Towey, forty-one, as their next-door neighbour. Frances's youngest brother John was one year old in 1910, which fits a man of forty-one in 1950, so this was very probably her brother: uncle and nephew living side by side.[^census-1910-towey][^census-1950-joseph-c] In 1950 Frances herself was working as a food handler at a public school.[^census-1950-frances]

people.summary: Named as Michael's child on his 1918 draft card, living at 216 Hamilton Street, Bridgeport. Not the same person as Dorothy Hennessey Belfiore, Seb's grandmother.
people.story:
Everything known about this Dorothy comes from one line. On September 12, 1918, her father Michael named "(Child) Dorothy Belfiore", of 216 Hamilton Street, Bridgeport, Connecticut, as his nearest relative.[^ww1-michael] Family knowledge holds that she was the daughter of Michael's first marriage.[^family-knowledge]

She is easy to confuse with another Dorothy Belfiore: Dorothy Hennessey, who married Michael's son Joseph and is Seb's grandmother. They are different women, a generation apart.

## What happened to her?

She has not been found in any later record. Earlier versions of this site suggested she died in the 1918 influenza epidemic, which did reach Bridgeport within two weeks of Michael's registration.[^ctx-flu-ct] That is possible, but nothing yet supports it. Her absence from Michael's household in 1940 means little, because by then she would have been an adult and may have married. She may also have been raised by her mother's family in Bridgeport.

Her birth year is not known. Earlier versions of the tree showed about 1914, without a source, and the card here keeps that estimate with a question mark.

Update, November 2026. Dorothy did grow up. In April 1930 she was seventeen and living with her father, her stepmother Frances and her little half-brothers Edward and Joseph in New Rochelle, working as a manicurist in a beauty shop. The census says she was born in New York about 1913, and that her mother, too, was born in New York.[^census-1930-michael] Where she lived in 1918 is still a question; her aunt Phyl's family had been in Bridgeport in 1910, and it is possible she stayed with relatives there.[^census-1910-paternostro]

Update, November 2026. Her father's 1918 draft card placed her at 216 Hamilton Street, Bridgeport; by 1930 she was at home with him at 52 Brook Street, New Rochelle.[^ww1-michael][^census-1930-michael]

Dorothy did not die young. As Dorothy Florence Racine she lived to 91. Social Security records give her birth as 1 February 1913, which fits the 1930 census, and a 2004 obituary index names her maiden name Belfiore and her birthplace New Rochelle.[^numident-dorothy-racine][^obit-index-dorothy-racine-2004] She married Joseph Anton Racine, and their son Joseph Francis Michael Racine, probably named in part for her father Michael, was born in Port Chester in 1940 and grew up in Yonkers, where Dorothy's aunt Mary D'Onofrio's family lived.[^obit-joseph-racine-2024] Dorothy died on 25 September 2004 in Morris Township, New Jersey, near her son's home, and was buried in the Bronx.[^obit-index-dorothy-racine-2004]

people.story:
Edward Belfiore appears in one record in this collection. On April 3, 1940, the census taker found him at 488 North Avenue, New Rochelle, with his parents Michael and Frances and his younger brother Joseph. He was nineteen and single, had completed two years of high school, and was out of school. He was listed as a "new worker", looking for his first job, and had earned nothing in 1939.[^census-1940]

His age places his birth between April 1920 and April 1921, in New York. Earlier versions of this site gave about 1923.

He would have been of draft age during the Second World War, and should have registered in 1941 or 1942. Nothing after 1940 has been found yet.

Update, November 2026. Edward was born on 21 March 1921. He served in the Army through the whole of the Second World War, from November 1941 to November 1945, and came home a corporal. He died on 4 February 1992 and rests in the Southern Nevada Veterans Memorial Cemetery at Boulder City.[^ssdi-numident-family][^edward-va-burial]

people.summary: Michael and Frances's younger son and Seb's grandfather, born in New York around 1922. He married Dorothy Hennessey and raised four children. Not Joe Belfore the golfer, his uncle.
people.story:
In April 1940 Joseph Belfiore was seventeen, in his second year of high school, and working fourteen hours a week as a delivery boy for a grocery store. He lived with his parents, Michael and Frances, and his brother Edward at 488 North Avenue in New Rochelle.[^census-1940]

That census age places his birth between April 1922 and April 1923, in New York. Earlier versions of this site gave about 1928, without a source. The census is better evidence, and the dates shown here follow it.

## Two Josephs

The family has two men named Joseph in consecutive generations, and they are easy to mix up. Joe Belfore the golfer, head professional at the Country Club of Detroit, was Michael's brother. This Joseph was Michael's son. Earlier versions of this site said he was named after this uncle, following the Italian custom of naming sons after relatives. That is likely, but no record states it. The golfer used the spelling Belfore; this Joseph kept Belfiore.

## Family

He married Dorothy Hennessey, who is remembered as Irish-American. They had four children: Robert, Seb's father; William; Karen; and Beth.[^family-knowledge]

He died in 1986. The family places his death in Valrico, Florida. A Social Security Death Index entry for a Joseph Belfiore who died in April 1986 gives a last residence in West Babylon, New York, and a number issued in Maryland. That entry has not been confirmed as his, and the two places need reconciling.[^family-knowledge][^ssdi-joseph]

Update, November 2026. Joseph was born on 1 December 1922 in New Rochelle. His first Social Security application, made at fifteen, gives his name as Joseph Anthony and his parents as Michael Belfiore and Frances Towey; later forms show him as Joseph C.[^ssaci-joseph-1922] The New Jersey death index records a Joseph C. Belfiore, born that same day, who died in Princeton on 19 October 1994, the year his wife Dorothy moved there.[^nj-death-1994-joseph][^obit-dorothy-2008] The family's memory of Valrico, Florida stays with his story as family tradition.

Update, November 2026. In 1930, aged seven, Joseph lived with his parents at 52 Brook Street.[^census-1930-michael] In April 1950 he was twenty-seven, a field mechanic for a lighting company, married to Dorothy and living in New Rochelle; next door lived John J. Towey, a lineman for a lighting company, who was very probably his uncle, his mother's youngest brother. Perhaps the uncle helped the nephew into the trade.[^census-1950-joseph-c][^census-1910-towey]

people.story:
Dorothy Hennessey married Joseph Belfiore, Michael's son, and was the mother of Robert, William, Karen and Beth. The family remembers her as Irish-American.[^family-knowledge]

She shares a name with an earlier Dorothy Belfiore: Michael's daughter from his first marriage, who was living in Bridgeport in 1918. They are different women. This Dorothy is Seb's grandmother.

Update, November 2026. Dorothy's obituary in Princeton's Town Topics says she was born in New Rochelle, lived most of her life in Babylon, Long Island, and worked twenty-five years for the Town of Babylon. She moved to Princeton in 1994 and died there on 5 January 2008, aged eighty-five, the widow of Joseph C. Belfiore.[^obit-dorothy-2008]

Update, November 2026. The 1950 census shows Dorothy, twenty-eight, and Joseph, twenty-seven, keeping house in New Rochelle.[^census-1950-joseph-c]

Family story. Dorothy's mother died young, and she was raised by her grandfather Patrick Hennessy and his second wife, Annie.[^family-knowledge]

Update, November 2026. The paper agrees with that story, and it does not yet name her father. She is missing from Patrick and Annie's house in 1925. In 1930 the census writes her as G-Daughter, age 8, born in New York, with a father and a mother who were both born in New York. In 1940 she is the grandchild, age 18. Patrick was born in Ireland, so those parental birthplaces do not fit him as her father. When she married Joseph C. Belfiore in May 1946, the New Rochelle paper called her Miss Dorothy Eleanore Hennessy, daughter of Patrick J. Hennessy, of Premium Point. The state index says 12 May 1946, certificate 23239. Another index line calls her father Joseph P. Hennessy. That line is kept, and it is not followed. Of Patrick's older sons, Joseph and Henry are the two the ages allow. Thomas, a lawyer with no children in 1930, is not her father. Later obituaries of Annie's children name Dorothy as a sister, among seven Hennessy children raised together: James, Frank, Catherine, Dorothy, Anne, Maria and Patricia. Anne remembered that the sisters stayed close all their lives and went to the theater and out to lunch together. Anne, the last of them, celebrated her 100th birthday in 2023. The tree does not draw Patrick and Annie as her parents, and it does not name a father who is not yet proved.[^hennessy-census-1925][^hennessy-census-1930-image][^hennessy-census-1940-image][^hennessy-marriage-announcement-1946][^hennessy-marriage-index-1946][^hennessy-marriage-index-joseph-p][^hennessy-thomas-1930][^obit-patricia-dillon-2021][^obit-francis-hennessy-2013][^obit-anne-latino-2024]

Update, November 2026. Joseph W. Hennessy, who died at New Rochelle on 22 March 1930, certificate 16632, is a lead for her father, not a proved identification. The index does not give his age.[^nys-death-index-hennessy-new-rochelle]

people.summary: Born in New Rochelle in 1897, one of the three golfing brothers. He ran the golf shop at the Seabreeze club in Daytona Beach alongside Sammy, and died in Daytona Beach in 1968.
people.story:
The one photograph in this collection that names Frank shows him behind the counter of a golf shop in Daytona Beach in early 1948. He stands on the right, in a pale shirt, with his brother Sammy across the room. The magazine caption reads, simply, "Sammy Belfore and (R) brother Frank in Seabreeze shop".[^golfdom-1948-02] In the article beside it Sammy wrote that his new, well-equipped golf shop would be under the supervision of his brother Frank.[^golfdom-1948-02]

Frank was born in New Rochelle in November 1897, about eleven months after his mother reached New York. An indexed record names his parents as Antonio Belfiore and Maria D. Circelli.[^frank-index] He was one of three brothers who became golf professionals, at a time when, as Sammy's obituary put it, the profession was dominated by men from abroad.[^standard-star-obit]

Little else about his career is documented here. Sammy's obituary says that "Frank took over the golf shop at the club in Daytona".[^standard-star-obit] Earlier research found that he died in Daytona Beach on April 21, 1968.[^frank-death] By the time Sammy died in 1972, Frank was described as dead.[^standard-star-obit]

A family photograph of three men in light suits on a golf course is believed to show Sammy, Frank and Joe together. Nobody in it has been identified with certainty.[^golf-brothers-photo]

Update, November 2026. Frank's own draft card of February 1942 gives his birthday as 31 October 1897, in New Rochelle. He was living in Grosse Pointe Park, Michigan, a few minutes from his brother Joe, whom he named as the person who would always know where to find him.[^ww2-frank] His name is also on New Rochelle's honor roll of the men who served in the First World War.[^nrpl-ww1-honor-roll]

Update, November 2026. In 1942 Frank lived at 1200 Grayton in Grosse Pointe Park and worked on Kercheval near Conner in Detroit; for the person who would always know his address he named his brother Joe, on Merriweather in Grosse Pointe Farms.[^ww2-frank] Before that he had grown up at the family's homes on Lawton Street, Brook Street and Albemarle in New Rochelle.[^census-1900][^census-1910][^census-1925]

Reports that Sammy, 72, died in Daytona Beach after a long illness; that he had changed the spelling of his name and had long been pro at the Seabreeze Golf and Tennis Club; that he was born on Christmas Day 1899 in New Rochelle to "the late Anthony and Maria Cicelli Belfiore", one of four brothers and five sisters; that Sammy, Frank and Joseph took up golf professionally when most pros were foreign-born; that Sam started as assistant pro at Wykagyl Country Club and went to Seabreeze in 1948 after 36 years in golf; that Frank ran the golf shop at the Daytona club and Joe was pro at Grosse Pointe, Michigan; that Frank, Joe and "their non-golfing brother, Michael" had died. people.summary: Head professional at the Country Club of Detroit for many years, author of Golfing Aids (1940), and by earlier research a two-time Michigan PGA champion. Not to be confused with his nephew Joseph, Seb's grandfather.
people.story:
In 1940 the professional at the Country Club of Detroit published a slim green booklet of lessons, priced at twenty-five cents. The title page reads Golfing Aids, by Joe Belfore, Professional, Country Club of Detroit. One surviving copy is signed "Sincerely, Joe Belfore, Detroit, Michigan, April 4, 1940", beside a photograph of the author in a white shirt and tie, his chin resting on his hand. It opens with the grip and stance, and its pages show him demonstrating the drive and a fairway wood.[^golfing-aids-1940] That copy came from the PGA REACH collection and was sold in 2025 with a letter of provenance signed by Bob Denney, the PGA of America's historian emeritus.[^pga-reach-letter-2025]

Joe was one of three Belfiore brothers from New Rochelle who became golf professionals, at a time when most professionals and club makers in America were from abroad, "usually Scotch", as Sammy's obituary put it.[^standard-star-obit] Like Sammy, he wrote the name Belfore.

## Florida winters, Michigan summers

In January 1929 he was working as a professional at Daytona Highlands in Florida, the same club as Sammy. At a tournament at Mount Plymouth that month, his pairing finished on 150, level with Sammy's.[^dbnj-1929-01-07] Like many northern club professionals, he seems to have worked in Florida for the winter season.

His main post was the Country Club of Detroit in Grosse Pointe Farms, Michigan, where he was head professional and ran the golf shop.[^golfing-aids-1940][^ccd-minutes-1963] Earlier research, drawing on the Michigan PGA's centennial history, records that he won the Michigan PGA championship in 1933 and 1937 and served as president of the Michigan PGA in 1959 and 1960. The same research found him in the field for the 1927 Metropolitan Open with Walter Hagen and Gene Sarazen, and in Golfdom magazine in January 1934.[^mipga-centennial][^nyt-1927][^golfdom-1934-01] In May 1948 the Daytona Beach papers reported that he had qualified for the PGA tournament at St. Louis.[^dbmj-1948-05-21]

## 1963

Joe died in 1963 after a long illness. On October 29 the club's Board of Governors set up a committee to find a professional "for the position of Golf Professional left vacant by the death of Joe Belfore". Mrs. Belfore had written the board a letter of appreciation. The board voted her $750 "as a gift to her" to help with debts from his illness, let her keep the golf shop open through Christmas until January 2, 1964, and paid his assistant, Danny Bianco, to carry on through the winter. It also gave his two sons, David and Joseph F. Jr., known as Jeffery, two years of personal golfing privileges at the club.[^ccd-minutes-1963]

## Two Josephs

This Joe is Seb's great-great-uncle. Seb's grandfather, also Joseph, was the son of Joe's brother Michael. Earlier versions of this site said the younger Joseph was named after this uncle, following the Italian custom of naming sons after relatives. That is likely, but no record states it.

Update, November 2026. Joe's draft card gives his full name, Joseph Francis Belfore, and his birthday, 5 February 1904, in New Rochelle; the person who would always know his address was his sister, Miss Rose Belfore, back home.[^ww2-joe] He had turned professional young: the 1925 census already lists him, at twenty-one, as a golf pro, and in 1931 a Washington paper noted "young Joe Belfore of New Rochelle" finishing third in the West Coast Open.[^census-1925][^evening-star-1931-03-01] He went on to win the Michigan PGA Championship in 1933 and 1937, served as the section's president in 1959 and 1960, and was twice its Professional of the Year.[^mipga-records] In the spring of 1941 Golfdom noted that the Joe Belfores were admiring a new baby boy.[^golfdom-1941-04] He died in October 1963 after a long illness; Golfdom's tribute followed in January.[^ccd-minutes-1963][^obit-index-joe-1963][^golfdom-1964-01]

Update, November 2026: Joe's home and more from Golfdom. Joe's 1942 card gives his home as 276 Merriweather in Grosse Pointe Farms, telephone Niagara 3226, and the club at 330 Country Club Drive; the 1950 census taker wrote the same house number, 276, beside his name. His brother Frank wrote "200 Merriweather" for him on his own card, probably a slip of memory.[^ww2-joe][^census-1950-joe][^ww2-frank] Golfdom kept noticing him: in October 1933, on Al Watrous's testimonial day at Oakland Hills, Joe partnered Watrous against Horton Smith and Frank Walsh and lost only on the 18th green, then spoke at the dinner that evening; in January 1960 he was Michigan's nominee for national Golf Professional of the Year; and that June, as president of the Michigan PGA, he gave a lesson and clinic for three hundred public-course golfers.[^golfdom-1934-01][^golfdom-1960-01][^golfdom-1960-06]

His obituary in the Detroit Free Press of 25 October 1963, as indexed, gives his death as 21 October 1963 in Grosse Pointe Farms and names his wife Ruth and his sons David and Jeff.[^obit-index-joe-belfore-1963-survivors]

Update, November 2026: in July 1934, between his two Michigan PGA titles, a "Belfore" came within one stroke of winning the Michigan Open at Saginaw Country Club. The Detroit Free Press headline the next morning read "Jake Fassezke Beats Belfore by Stroke to Win State Open".[^dfp-1934-michigan-open] Joe, then the professional at the Country Club of Detroit, is almost certainly the Belfore meant, though the article itself has not yet been read.

media.transcription:
COUNTRY CLUB OF DETROIT. MINUTES OF MEETING OF THE BOARD OF GOVERNORS. HELD: OCTOBER 29, 1963.
[Page 265] GOLF, GROUNDS AND GREENS COMMITTEE

Mr. Barr announced the formation of a Committee consisting of Charles G. Chapman, Chairman, A. Fred Kammer, Jr., George Haggarty, Carlton M. Higbie, Jr., and Mrs. Harley G. Higbie, for the purpose of interviewing applicants for the position of Golf Professional left vacant by the death of Joe Belfore. The Committee will report its recommendations to the Board, however, selection of the new Golf Professional is to be made by the Board.

Mr. Higbie presented the letter of appreciation from Mrs. Belfore, and a general discussion was had regarding the handling of the Golf Shop and closing the Club accounts with the Estate of Joe Belfore. After discussion it was unanimously agreed that the Club would pay to Mrs. Belfore the sum of Seven hundred and fifty Dollars ($750.00) as a gift to her and to assist her in the settlement of obligations resulting from the long illness of her husband. On the recommendation of Mr. Higbie it was agreed that the Club would pay the sum of One thousand dollars ($1000.00) to Danny Bianco, Assistant Golf Professional, for services rendered during the past golfing season, and in addition, pay him Four hundred dollars ($400.00) for each of the months of January and February of 1964, and Two hundred dollars ($200.00) for the first half of March. Mr. Higbie stated that the Golf Shop would stay open for the Christmas Season and his recommendation that Mrs. Belfore be permitted to continue the Shop until January 2, 1964, was unanimously approved.

A discussion was had regarding the question whether and to what extent golfing privileges should be extended to David and Joseph F., Jr. (Jeffery) Belfore, sons of Joe Belfore.

On recommendation of Mr. Higbie, it was unanimously agreed that golfing privileges limited to them personally and not to guests or members of their respective families be granted to David and Jeffery Belfore, for a period of two (2) years from and after November 1, 1963. Both men shall have the right to sign chits for themselves and have the use of the Men's Grill and Locker Room.

The only document about Joe's wife in this collection is the Country Club of Detroit's board minutes of October 29, 1963, written after Joe's death. They call her Mrs. Belfore. She had sent the board a letter of appreciation. The board voted her $750 as a gift, to help with the debts left by her husband's long illness, and agreed that she could keep the golf shop open through the Christmas season, until January 2, 1964.[^ccd-minutes-1963]

The minutes name her sons as David and Joseph F. Jr., known as Jeffery.[^ccd-minutes-1963] Earlier versions of the tree gave her first name as Ruth, but no source for it is recorded, so it is marked as unverified here.

Update, November 2026. In 1950 Ruth's mother, Beulah M. Burdick, a widow born in Wisconsin, was living with Joe and Ruth in Grosse Pointe Woods; Ruth herself was born in Minnesota.[^census-1950-joe]

people.summary: Born in New Rochelle on Christmas Day 1899, the first of the three golfing brothers. A Wykagyl shop boy who became a club professional in Duluth and Daytona Beach, taught a blind golfer to play, and later ran the 19th Hole bar on Seabreeze Boulevard.
people.story:
Sammy Belfore stood, by one sports editor's account, "just a fraction over five feet", powerfully built, with a white crest of hair and thick black eyebrows. He wore a silk ascot as a trademark. He would challenge a man to eighteen holes using only a two iron, for a side bet, and win. In his later years he was known to give a useful lesson without getting off his bar stool.[^kahn-1965][^willson-1970] He was born in New Rochelle on Christmas Day 1899, one of the nine children of Anthony and Maria Belfiore.[^standard-star-obit]

## Wykagyl

He started in golf at thirteen, in the golf shop at Wykagyl Country Club in New Rochelle, and was giving lessons by sixteen.[^kahn-1960] He told a reporter years later that he had worked in the shop for "the immortal Alex Smith", and had to wait until the members were off the course before he could sneak in a few holes before dark.[^willson-1970] Smith was a Scottish professional who won the US Open in 1906 and again in 1910, when the New York Times called him the Wykagyl professional.[^ctx-alex-smith]

That background is why the family story matters. Sammy's obituary explained that before the Belfiore brothers, golf professionals and club makers in America were almost all foreign-born, usually Scots. Sam was the first of the three American-born brothers to break through, as assistant professional at Wykagyl.[^standard-star-obit]

## White Sulphur Springs and Florida

He went on to be head professional at White Sulphur Springs, the West Virginia resort now called the Greenbrier. The Daytona papers later reported that he once beat Walter Hagen there by a stroke in a head-to-head match in 1922, and that Sam Snead succeeded him at the resort. Both stories come from Sammy's own recollections as retold in print.[^willson-1966][^kahn-1965][^dben-1972-02-16]

He began spending winters in Daytona Beach in the 1920s. In January 1929 the News-Journal described him as "the diminutive professional at Daytona Highlands", after he shot the best individual round, a 71, at a tournament at Mount Plymouth. His brother Joe was also listed as a Daytona Highlands professional.[^dbnj-1929-01-07] Accounts disagree on when he settled for good: one column says 1924, his news obituary 1938.[^kahn-1960][^dben-1972-02-16]

## Duluth and the blind golfer

In May 1930 his engagement to Virginia Hupp was announced in Detroit by her mother, Mrs. Mae Hupp. The wedding was planned for late June at her mother's home, and the couple were to live in Duluth, Minnesota, in the summer and in Daytona Beach in the winter.[^engagement-1930]

Duluth was his summer job. He was the professional at Ridgeview Country Club there, and it was at Ridgeview that he began teaching Clinton Russell, a Duluth businessman who had been blinded in 1924 when a tire exploded in his face. Between them they worked out a method in which a caddie or friend teed the ball, set his stance for direction and lined up the clubface. In 1931 Russell shot 84 at Ridgeview, and Ripley's Believe It or Not ran the story. On August 20, 1938, Russell beat the English blind golfer W. H. J. Oxenham at Ridgeview, a match that made Time magazine.[^ouse-russell]

Earlier versions of this site put Ridgeview in Westchester and the 1938 match at Wykagyl. The Russell biography in this collection places both in Duluth.

## Daytona Beach

He was head professional at the Daytona Beach Country Club through the 1930s and into the 1940s. On March 13, 1946, he arranged a free exhibition there for Jimmy Demaret, Ben Hogan, Sam Snead and Byron Nelson. Some 4,200 people followed it, and Demaret shot 63. Fourteen years later Sammy could still recount the round shot by shot, and remembered that he had set the pins in difficult places.[^kahn-1960]

In 1947 he oversaw the restoration of the Seabreeze Golf Club for its owner, Earl Warner, and became its pro-manager when it reopened on January 1, 1948, with his brother Frank running the shop. He described the job that February in Golfdom, the golf trade magazine.[^golfdom-1948-02][^golfdom-1948-01][^kahn-1965] The local sports editor later wrote that after dark the clubhouse was a gambling house, and that some of the men who worked for it wore shoulder holsters.[^kahn-1965]

## The 19th Hole

When the club closed, he opened a bar on Seabreeze Boulevard and called it the 19th Hole. The papers give different years for the change, from 1947 to 1951.[^kahn-1960][^kahn-1965][^dben-1972-02-16] A 1951 directory listing put it at 324 Seabreeze Boulevard, as a cocktail lounge, bar and package store.[^research-notes] He held court there for years. The jukebox played "Straight Down the Middle", and one night Rocky Marciano, retired and unbeaten, came in to see him.[^kahn-1965][^dben-1972-02-16] Marciano's mother came from San Bartolomeo in Galdo, the town Sammy's parents had left.[^ctx-marciano] Whether either man knew that is not recorded.

He was a gambler. The same sports editor wrote that he once walked out of a dice game with $27,000 and lost it all the next afternoon on a horse-racing parlay. "I've got nobody to blame but myself," Sammy would say.[^kahn-1965] In March 1965 the sheriff padlocked the bankrupt 19th Hole, and Sammy suffered a severe heart attack the same day.[^kahn-1965][^kahn-1972]

He recovered and lived quietly at 11 South Hollywood Avenue. He died at Halifax Hospital early on Wednesday, February 16, 1972, after a stroke.[^dben-1972-02-16] A requiem Mass was said at Our Lady of Lourdes Church and he was buried at Cedar Hill Memory Gardens.[^dben-1972-02-17]

## Family

His marriage to Virginia Hupp produced a daughter, Patricia Hupp Belfore, born in 1933.[^patricia-findagrave] The marriage ended around 1939, according to earlier research.[^patricia-obit] In November 1948 the Morning Journal announced a fourth birthday party for "Little Sammy Belfore", given by his mother, Mrs. Sammy Belfore, at their home at 217 Jessamine Boulevard. A city directory entry noted in Seb's research lists Sam Belfore at that address with a wife named Louisa.[^dbmj-1948-11-20][^research-notes] His survivors in 1972 were his son Samuel M. Belfore, his daughter Mrs. Patricia Fleming of Birmingham, Michigan, five sisters, and several nieces, including a Mrs. Angelia Carr.[^dben-1972-02-17]

## The name

Sammy is the brother documented as changing the spelling: his New Rochelle obituary says he "had changed the spelling of his name".[^standard-star-obit] Family tradition holds that the shorter Belfore was chosen to fit on golf scorecards. No document in this collection records the reason.[^family-knowledge]

Update, November 2026. Sammy's own World War I draft card, filled in in September 1918 when he was nineteen, describes him as a golf instructor working for Alex Smith at Wykagyl in New Rochelle, the club where the family always said he started.[^ww1-samuel] In February 1942 he registered again in Daytona Beach. That card gives his birthday as 25 December 1898, a year earlier than the family date, and shows him working at the Shenecossett Country Club in New London, Connecticut; the person who would always know his address was Mrs. Virginia H. Belfore of Birmingham, Michigan.[^ww2-samuel] The family's Christmas Day 1899 stays as his birthday here, with 1898 noted beside it.

Update, November 2026: Sammy's addresses. His 1918 card gives 41 Brook Street, New Rochelle, the family home, with his father Tony at the same address. In February 1942 he lived at 1517 South Atlantic Avenue in Daytona Beach and collected his mail at Box 3603, while Virginia stayed at 251 West Maple Avenue in Birmingham, Michigan.[^ww1-samuel][^ww2-samuel] By April 1950 he was the proprietor of a cocktail lounge in Daytona Beach, married to Louisa.[^census-1950-samuel]

media.summary: Summary. Sammy Belfore, pro-manager at the Seabreeze Golf & Tennis Club, Daytona Beach, writes about running a winter pro shop as a test market for the coming northern season. He describes the rebuilt club, which reopened on January 1 (1948) under Earl Warner after years of dormancy: a nine-hole course of 3,107 yards, reseeding that cost $4,600, and a renovated clubhouse. He writes that his new golf shop is under the supervision of his brother Frank. A photograph shows Sammy and, at right, his brother Frank in the Seabreeze shop.

media.summary: Summary. Biography of Clinton Russell (1895-1961), a Duluth businessman blinded in 1924 when a tire exploded as he changed it. A few years later he took lessons from Sammy Belfore, the pro at Duluth's Ridgeview Country Club, and worked out a system with a caddie or friend who teed the ball and set his stance. He shot 84 at Ridgeview in 1931, which Ripley's Believe It or Not reported in 1932, and beat W. H. J. Oxenham of England at Ridgeview on August 20, 1938, in a match noted by Time magazine. His regular caddie was Jimmy Koehler.

people.summary: Sammy's first wife, a 1927 graduate of the State Normal College at Ypsilanti. They married in 1930, and she was the mother of Patricia Hupp Fleming.
people.story:
Virginia Hupp's engagement to Sam Belfore was announced in May 1930 by her mother, Mrs. Mae Hupp. The wedding was set for late June at her mother's home, 251 West Maple Avenue, and the couple planned to spend summers in Duluth, Minnesota, and winters in Daytona Beach.[^engagement-1930]

The announcement says she had attended St. Mary's Academy at Monroe for two years, graduated from Baldwin High School and, in 1927, from the State Normal College at Ypsilanti, and had since done graduate work at the University of Michigan. She had spent a season in Daytona Beach two years earlier. At the engagement party a centerpiece of white sweet peas, shaped like a large golf ball, opened to reveal the couple's cards.[^engagement-1930]

Their daughter, Patricia Hupp Belfore, was born in 1933.[^patricia-findagrave] Earlier research found that the marriage ended around 1939 and that Virginia later married John Moss.[^patricia-obit]

Earlier versions of this site linked her family to the Hupp Motor Car Company of Detroit, maker of the Hupmobile. No document in this collection makes that link, so it is marked as unverified.

Update, November 2026. When Sammy registered for the draft in Daytona Beach in February 1942, the person he named was Mrs. Virginia H. Belfore of 251 West Maple Avenue, Birmingham, Michigan: the same street address that their 1930 engagement notice gave for her mother's home (the notice says Detroit; the draft card shows it was Birmingham, a suburb north of Detroit). The address ties the two records together and suggests Virginia was staying with her mother in Michigan that winter.[^ww2-samuel][^engagement-1930]

people.story:
Rose is known from her brother Sammy's obituaries. In February 1972 the Standard-Star listed "the Misses Rose and Caroline Belfiore of Wykagyl Gardens" among his survivors, and the Daytona Beach funeral notice listed "Miss Rose Belfore".[^standard-star-obit][^dben-1972-02-17] She was unmarried and living with her sister Caroline in New Rochelle.

Wykagyl is the New Rochelle neighborhood around the country club where Sammy had started in golf. Her birth year is not documented; earlier versions of the tree showed about 1903 without a source.

Update, November 2026. Rose was born on 3 June 1900 and stayed in New Rochelle all her life; in 1930 she was a stenographer, and in 1950 she and her sister Carolyn kept house together.[^ssdi-numident-family][^census-1930][^census-1950-rose] When her brother Joe registered for the draft in Michigan, it was Rose he named as the person who would always know where he was.[^ww2-joe] She died in March 1994.[^ssdi-numident-family]

Update, November 2026. When her brother Joe registered for the draft in 1942, he named Rose, at the Wykagyl Gardens Apartments in New Rochelle, as the person who would always know where he was. She and Carolyn were still at Wykagyl Gardens in 1972, so Rose made her home there for at least thirty years, in the Wykagyl neighbourhood where Sammy had started in golf at the Wykagyl club.[^ww2-joe][^standard-star-obit] In 1950 she was the head of the household, a secretary, with Carolyn beside her.[^census-1950-rose]

people.summary: One of the five Belfiore sisters. Her full name was Philomena; she married Angelo Paternostro and lived in Hartford, Connecticut.
people.story:
Earlier versions of this site guessed that Phyl was short for Phyllis or Filomena. The Daytona Beach funeral notice for her brother Sammy settles it: it lists "Mrs. Philomena Paternoster" among his sisters. New Rochelle's Standard-Star gave her as "Mrs. Angelo (Phyl) Paternostro, Hartford, Conn."[^dben-1972-02-17][^standard-star-obit] The two papers spell her married name differently.

She married Angelo Paternostro and in 1972 lived in Hartford. Philomena is also a name that Italian families often shortened to Lena, which makes her a second candidate for the Lena Belfiore of an indexed record.[^lena-index]

Update, November 2026. Phyl was the eldest daughter. Born in San Bartolomeo in September 1887, she was the little "Francesca, nine" who crossed on the Oregon with her mother in December 1896, and the New Rochelle census takers wrote her name as Filomena, Philmenia and even Willmena.[^oregon-1896-manifest][^census-1900][^census-1905][^census-1920] On 20 January 1906 she married Angelo Paternoster in New Rochelle.[^marriage-index-1906]

Phyl's own family can now be traced. By 1910 she and Angelo had settled in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with a daughter, Marianna, and a baby son, Dominick. Ten years later they were in Hartford, where they raised five children: Marian, Dominick, Dorothy, Anthony and Carl. By 1930 they owned their home, and by 1940 Phyl had become an American citizen.[^census-1910-paternostro][^census-1920-paternostro][^census-1930-paternostro][^census-1940-paternostro] Her brother Michael's daughter Dorothy was living in Bridgeport in 1918, and it is possible she was close to her aunt's family there; that is still a lead.

Update, November 2026: Phyl's homes. In 1910 she and Angelo rented at 35 Hallett Street in Bridgeport; in 1920 they lived on Goodman Place in Hartford; and by 1930 they owned 397 Woodland Street, Hartford, where they were still living in 1940.[^census-1910-paternostro][^census-1920-paternostro][^census-1930-paternostro][^census-1940-paternostro]

Phyl died in April 1972. Her obituary in the Hartford Courant of 23 April 1972, as indexed, names her husband Angelo, her children Dominic F., Albert A. and Carl D. Paternostro, Mary Bird and Dorothy Ryalls, and her sisters Mary D'Onofrio, Rose Belfiore, Carolyn Belfiore and Molly Drew. It is the only record found that names the Belfiore sisters together.[^obit-index-filomena-paternostro-1972][^ct-death-index-paternostro]

people.summary: One of the five Belfiore sisters. She married Joseph D'Onofrio and in 1972 lived in Hollywood, Florida.
people.story:
Mary is listed in her brother Sammy's obituaries as "Mrs. Joseph (Mary) D'Onofrio of Hollywood, Fla." and "Mrs. Mary D'Onofrio".[^standard-star-obit][^dben-1972-02-17] Nothing else about her is documented here yet.

Update, November 2026. Mary was born in San Bartolomeo in October 1889 and crossed on the Oregon at six, listed as Anna.[^census-1900][^oregon-1896-manifest] On 10 December 1911 she married Joseph (Giuseppe) D'Onofrio in New Rochelle.[^marriage-index-1911] The D'Onofrio family remembers that the couple settled in Millburn, New Jersey, and raised six children: Leonard, Angelina, Frank, Donald, Raymond and Dolores.[^donofrio-post-2010] Two of their sons' Social Security records name their mother as Mary Belfore or Belfiore.[^ssdi-numident-family]

The censuses fill in the family's homes. Their two eldest, Leonard and Angelina, were born in New Jersey, which fits the D'Onofrio family's memory of New Jersey; by 1920 the family was in Yonkers, where they stayed through 1940, owning their home by 1930.[^census-1920-donofrio][^census-1930-donofrio][^census-1940-donofrio] The family's memory of Millburn is kept here too: the censuses have not yet found them there, but it may belong to the New Jersey years or to later life.[^donofrio-post-2010] In 1910, just before her marriage, Mary seems to appear at home as "Mattie, daughter, eighteen, born in Italy, came in 1896"; with Michael and Phyl living elsewhere, that makes exactly the nine children her mother reported.[^census-1910]

Update, November 2026: Mary's homes. In 1920 Mary and Joseph rented at 23 Lockwood Avenue, Yonkers; by 1930 they owned 91 Buckingham Road; and in 1940 they rented on Beech Street.[^census-1920-donofrio][^census-1930-donofrio][^census-1940-donofrio]

Update, November 2026: the Westchester County Archives index also lists her wedding, as Maria Belfiore and Giuseppe D'Onofrio, under one certificate number in 1911.[^westchester-marriage-index] And it lists a naturalization petition of 1943 by Mary D'Onofrio, with her maiden name Belfiore beside it.[^westchester-naturalization-index] That is a telling detail. As a child she had most likely become an American through her father's naturalization in 1899, but under the law of 1907 an American woman who married a foreign citizen lost her own citizenship. Joseph did not file his first papers until 1922, so Mary, who had lived in America since the age of six, had to apply in her own name. The petition itself, not yet seen, should give her birth date and place and her arrival in 1896.

people.story:
An indexed record found in earlier research gives a Lena Belfiore, born about 1901, with parents Antonio Belfiore and Maria D. Circelli.[^lena-index] The Research page describes it as the 1940 census, but that cannot be right as written: the 1940 census does not record parents' names. The record behind the index needs to be identified.

Sammy's 1972 obituaries name nine children and no Lena.[^standard-star-obit][^dben-1972-02-17] So either Lena died before 1972, or she is one of the five sisters under a pet name. Lena is a common Italian short form of names such as Filomena and Carolina, and both Philomena (Phyl) and Caroline were among the sisters. Her link to the family is shown with a dashed line until a record settles it.

Update, November 2026. Lena is very likely Carolyn herself, called Lena as a girl (Lena is a common short form of Carolina). See Caroline's profile. Her card stays here until a record settles it.[^census-1915][^census-1920][^census-1925]
